newsitem.title: USA: Medical costs for U.S. business up 2.5 percent in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Medical costs for U.S. business up 2.5 percent in 1996.

text.p: Health care costs for U.S. businesses rose 2.5 percent in 1996, more slowly than consumer price inflation but faster than the 2.1 percent increase in 1995, consulting firm Foster Higgins reported on Tuesday.
Foster Higgins attributed the subdued rate of cost growth to the continuing shift of workers to mangaged care plans and declining coverage costs in health maintenance organisations.
It warned, however, that costs could grow more rapidly in the future if managed care premiums rise and the federal government cuts Medicare spending, shifting more costs to private payers.
In a nationwide survey of more than 3,200 employers, Foster Higgins found total health benefit costs averaged $3,915 per employee in 1996 compared with $3,821 in 1995, when costs rose 2.1 percent.

Foster Higgins said there was a shift to managed care plans, especially among small employers. It said the medical component of the consumer price index, which measures costs including doctors fees, prescription drug and hospital prices, rose 3.1 percent in 1996, less than overall inflation.
"HMO rates are rising for 1997, following two years of premium roll-backs and sagging profits," said Foster Higgins principal John Erb, the study's chief author.

In 1996, health maintenance organisation costs fell 2.2 percent to $3,185 per active employee, the survey found. But enrollment in traditional HMO plans also appeared to stall in 1996, while point-of-service plans continued to gain enrollees, the study said.
Erb also said many employers had also already enjoyed the one-time cost savings of moving employees out of more expensive traditional indemnity plans into managed care.
The survey said managed care plan cost has grown at a consistently slower pace over the last four years than indemnity plan cost.

Since 1993, indemnity plan cost for active and retired employees has risen a cumulative 19 percent, preferred provider organisation cost has risen 8 percent and HMO cost has risen 3 percent, Foster Higgens said.
The survey said average costs for large employers, or those with 500 or more workers, rose 3.6 percent in 1996, while costs fell 2 percent for smaller employers.
One factor slowing overall cost growth for business was the movement of retirees to managed care, Foster Higgins said.
Among large employers, over half of early retirees, or 52 percent, and 30 percent of those aged 65 and over were enrolled in managed care, it said.
"If retirees move rapidly into managed care over the next few years, the cost savings could help offset the increases we're predicting for active employees," Erb said.
